video_title: Bitcoin Is The Best Hedge Fund That's Ever Existed
gist: Jordi Visser tells Anthony Pompliano that the July blow-up of Leopold's roughly $25bn AI-focused hedge fund was a cleansing forced-liquidation inside a record factor and momentum unwind, and that hedge fund leverage is structurally topping out, guaranteeing more 'speed crashes'. He argues compute scarcity is real — Amazon, Microsoft and Google contracted backlogs nearing $2 trillion and everyone from Sam Altman to Dario Amodei admitting they underestimated needed supply — so he is buying scarcity (Micron, GE Vernova, Bitcoin) while predicting AI destroys the growth certainty, and therefore the multiples, of all public companies. He frames Bitcoin as the best-performing 'hedge fund' ever and predicts AI-agent allocation plus tokenization moves crypto from about $3 trillion to roughly $100 trillion out of a roughly fixed $700 trillion global wealth pool.

insights.claim: Visser says Leopold's fund losses began before any Citadel or prime-broker involvement, driven by an AI mid-cycle slowdown in which crowded positions all moved against the same holders at once and compounded too fast to manage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Attributing the drawdown to crowding rather than a conspiracy means the same setup can recur in any consensus AI book, so position-overlap screens matter more than headline risk.
insights.quote: the losses were happening because there was going to be a correction and things don't go straight up.

insights.claim: Once a levered fund reaches forced-liquidation stage, prime brokers at the investment banks circulate the portfolio to potential buyers, who then hedge their own overlapping exposure and accelerate the decline — the pattern Visser lived through in the 1998 LTCM unwind, the 2007 quant/GARP unwind and Archegos in 2021.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a repeatable playbook: once a large fund's holdings hit the press, expect a multi-day cascade in its most crowded names before stabilization.
insights.quote: your prime brokers know everything and they're calling people, which is normally what happens cuz the prime brokers at the investment banks are the lenders of these and once they're involved, everyone starts to see the portfolio

insights.claim: Visser characterizes the four-day slide that began Friday and ended in the two hours after the Fed decision as both liquidation of Leopold's book and opportunistic de-risking by funds with the same exposure, and calls it a cleansing event rather than the start of a bear market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames the drawdown as flow-driven and largely complete, arguing for buying weakness in AI names rather than treating the move as a fundamental repricing.
insights.quote: this was a cleansing event in my opinion

insights.claim: Leopold was rumored up roughly 400% through June on about $25 billion raised only two to three years ago, and even down 70-80% may retain around $10 billion, of which roughly $5 billion is reported to be a private Anthropic position.
insights.speaker: host (Anthony Pompliano) and Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A remaining ~$10bn with about half locked in illiquid private Anthropic stock implies the liquid public-equity selling is largely done, capping further forced supply.
insights.quote: out of the 10 billion, I mean, it's being reported that about 5 billion of that is private an anthropic position

insights.claim: Visser expects Leopold to struggle to raise institutional capital again despite still being up roughly 80% year to date, because a 25-year-old describing an 80% drawdown as a learning experience fails large-allocator diligence even though good returns normally attract money.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capital does not automatically recycle back to blown-up star managers, which slows re-leveraging of the crowded AI trade.
insights.quote: I think it's very hard to come back from a scenario where you're 25 years old and you're talking about you've just had a learning experience

themes.theme: Leverage regime shift and the post-flush setup

insights.claim: Hedge fund gross leverage entered 2026 at all-time highs, with Goldman Sachs data cited as the largest increase in gross exposure in any five-month period in history — occurring exactly as three-year terminal values were becoming unknowable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Peak leverage against collapsing forecastability is the core fragility, arguing for smaller size rather than levered dip-buying.
insights.quote: Goldman Sachs said it was the largest increase in gross exposure that they had seen in any 5-month period in history

insights.claim: Visser calls July a record factor unwind and the largest momentum unwind in history, caused by positions becoming more crowded than ever as AI agents and easy portfolio optimization push managers into the same trades.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crowding is now algorithmically reinforced, making factor-crowding metrics a primary risk input rather than a curiosity.
insights.quote: for the month of July we saw a record factor unwind

insights.claim: Visser's central market-structure call is that hedge fund leverage never returns to its recent highs because prime brokers will permanently extend less credit after events like Leopold's, mirroring how 20%-plus S&P 500 earnings growth this year still produced multiple compression rather than a 20% index gain.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Lower system leverage caps index multiples and thins liquidity in crowded names, a structural headwind even when earnings deliver.
insights.quote: The market structure is changing, and I don't think leverage is ever going to go back to the highs.

insights.claim: Visser predicts more frequent 'speed crashes' and more Leopold-style blow-ups because the innovation cycle has compressed — what used to take 30 years now takes 3 — while hedge funds still hold illiquid levered positions against quarterly liquidity terms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for owning optionality and keeping dry powder, since violent air-pockets become a recurring feature rather than tail events.
insights.quote: no matter how fast markets go up in a bubble, they look like you're going upstairs during it and then you fall down the elevator shoot on the way down

insights.claim: Visser says the bottom is in for the AI trade, and his 'Combing Through the Carnage' report screens for names that technically did not break down and have merely reset while holding above moving averages in what he still considers a bull market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit timing call with a screening method: favor AI names that held technical structure through the July liquidation.
insights.quote: I'm going to cover why I think the bottom is in for the AI trade

insights.claim: Visser quantifies the improved setup with his father's odds framing: in May the AI trade offered roughly one-to-two payoff over six months, whereas after the correction the odds on many names are now about three to one.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Converts the drawdown into an explicit payoff-odds threshold for adding exposure rather than a vibe-based dip buy.
insights.quote: if in May the odds on the AI trade working were one to two and you were barely getting any payoff over the next 6 months, you'll be shocked right now that with the correction we've had, which is still in a bull market

insights.claim: Visser disclosed buying Micron in 'nibbles' and adding lower after an initial purchase two weeks earlier, saying he is now more comfortable buying weakness than strength while still expecting more liquidations, particularly in the first week of August.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A dated expectation of further early-August forced selling paired with scaled buying gives both a calendar and an execution style to track.
insights.quote: I think there's going to be more of a more liquidations coming particularly in the first week of August

themes.theme: Compute scarcity vs the AI-overbuild narrative

insights.claim: Visser's core AI thesis is that compute demand will outstrip supply for a long time, and he notes that every builder close to actual demand contradicts the investor consensus that the industry has overbuilt and cannot earn the revenue back.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If scarcity rather than glut binds, sell-offs driven by overbuild fears are buying opportunities in compute and memory suppliers.
insights.quote: every single smart person that's involved with building this stuff and seeing the demand is saying they can't keep up with it

insights.claim: Amazon, Microsoft and Google's combined contracted-order backlog is nearing $2 trillion — over $2 trillion including Oracle — and all of them raised rather than cut CapEx on the latest calls while stating orders match the spend.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A ~$2trn contracted backlog is the hard rebuttal to the revenue-shortfall thesis and a reason to fade hyperscaler credit panic.
insights.quote: the total sum of their backlog of contracted orders is nearing 2 trillion. If you add in Oracle, you're over 2 trillion.

insights.claim: Visser endorses Dwarkesh's contrarian argument, echoed by Gavin Baker, that with finite compute the labs delivering the most efficient models — Anthropic and OpenAI — capture the largest orders because they were also smart enough to secure available compute, which cuts against the open-source disruption story.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies AI economics concentrate in two labs' ARR, so open-source-driven margin collapse may be the wrong short thesis.
insights.quote: if there's a finite amount of compute, the company that is able to deliver the most efficient models, which is what Anthropic and Open AR, they're going to take the big orders from everyone

insights.claim: Visser reframes AI cost with a gasoline analogy: at $1 a gallon buyers accept gas guzzlers, but at $10 a gallon they pay 50% more for a 40-mpg car — so scarce, expensive compute makes efficiency measured in tokens per watt the deciding purchase criterion.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for picking AI winners: efficiency per watt, not raw capability, decides who wins enterprise budgets while compute is tight.
insights.quote: the most valuable things are going to want tokens per watt

insights.claim: Visser illustrates compute allocation by willingness-to-pay with a Disney thought experiment — Disney bidding $1 trillion for a hypothetical 100 gigawatts of Anthropic compute versus $100 billion from everyone else — arguing firms with distribution and high revenue per token, especially in video, outbid everyone.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Points to content owners with pricing power as the marginal compute buyers and to video as the dominant token-demand driver.
insights.quote: the most token-hungry scenario is video

insights.claim: Visser distinguishes compute 'gobblers' from sellers: OpenAI and Anthropic consume everything available, xAI/SpaceX sells spare capacity only because humanoid and full-self-driving demand has not arrived yet, and Meta is holding capacity for personal agents.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reading who buys versus sells compute reveals each player's real roadmap timing and where spare capacity gets reabsorbed later.
insights.quote: Open AI and Anthropic are not offering out compute. They are the gobblers. They are the ones eating everything.

insights.claim: Every leading AI figure underestimated required compute supply: Sam Altman told Patrick O'Shaughnessy 'we underestimated the amount of supply', and Dario Amodei, who warned about ROIC last year, is now scrambling for capacity from SpaceX, which also sold capacity to a capacity-short Google whose Gemini has fallen behind.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If even Google must buy capacity from SpaceX, spare-capacity holders and physical compute suppliers hold unusual pricing power.
insights.quote: We underestimated the amount of supply.

insights.claim: Visser argues agentic inference demand has barely begun because only coding agents exist today, while personal agents require on-device memory and hardware that does not yet exist — Siri and Alexa still do not work, and phone-based models fail in weak cell coverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Points to a multi-year device memory and edge-silicon upgrade cycle as the next demand leg, supporting memory exposure.
insights.quote: we're not even out of the first out in the first inning of the agentic needs for inference. All we're doing so far are the coding agents.

insights.claim: Visser says China's open-source AI plan matters directly to investors, and drawing on Kevin Rudd's interview with Ezra Klein plus his own month-a-year travel to China from 2007 to 2012, that Beijing already owns the manufacturing base for the molecules-to-bits transition while expecting the West's K-shaped economy to push it toward socialism.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames Chinese manufacturing control as the strategic chokepoint in the AI buildout, relevant to supply-chain and energy-equipment exposure.
insights.quote: you really start to realize that most of what you hear in the Western media is not true

insights.claim: South Korea's stock market fell 45% in about 40 days, erasing $2 trillion of market cap, with roughly 1.2 million leveraged retail accounts margin-called by mid-July, while Japan saw about $200 billion wiped out in a single near-3% down day.
insights.speaker: host (Anthony Pompliano)
insights.so_what: Quantifies where forced retail deleveraging actually sits, letting investors treat Asian drawdowns as local leverage events rather than US signals.

insights.claim: Visser contextualizes the Korean crash by noting Korea is still up 56% year to date versus roughly 8% for the S&P 500, framing the collapse as a giveback of an outsized run rather than a systemic break.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Year-to-date framing changes the trade: a 45% drop from a much larger run is a positioning flush, not evidence of contagion into US equities.
insights.quote: Korea's up 56% year to date

insights.claim: Visser argues Korean retail needed leverage because non-US equities only broke above their 2007 levels in the last three years, giving those investors their first real bull market, whereas US households with over $180 trillion of net worth do not need the same leverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains why Asian retail margin cascades are unlikely to replicate in the US, arguing against reflexively hedging US exposure on Asian liquidations.
insights.quote: the household net worth in the country is over 180 trillion dollars

insights.claim: Visser says Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron multiples already embed an eventual cycle end, while physical constraints give them genuine scarcity — Micron is now earning margins at levels never before seen in memory.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory is priced as cyclical while behaving as scarce; that gap is the trade, and margin durability is the variable to monitor.
insights.quote: this is why Micron is having margins now at levels that we've never seen in memory because they have scarcity of it

insights.claim: Visser predicts AI will destroy the growth certainty of all public companies over five years — not bankrupt them, but make three-year survival unknowable as higher-margin AI-native startups attack every line of business — which is why equity multiples should structurally fall.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structural de-rating call: own scarcity and store-of-value assets rather than paying for terminal-value certainty that no longer exists.
insights.quote: AI will destroy all public companies. And when I say destroy, it will destroy the growth certainty of all companies going forward and that's why multiples should come down.

themes.theme: Warsh Fed, delevering and tokenized money supply

insights.claim: Visser supports Kevin Warsh's decision to hold and his rejection of old academic models, arguing that when every month behaves like 30 months, lagged inflation data can only serve as a psychological anchor for dealing with humans rather than a decision input.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A Fed reasoning from AI-driven speed rather than lagged data is less predictable, raising the volatility premium embedded in rates.
insights.quote: Kevin Warsh is saying the Fed needs to change because of AI.

insights.claim: The market response to Warsh was a steepening yield curve after he argued that rising 10-year and 2-year rates meant the market had already delivered the tightening while inflation eased, buying the Fed time to wait.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Signals the Fed will let market-driven tightening substitute for hikes, favoring curve-steepener expressions over outright hike bets.

insights.claim: Visser argues that dropping forward guidance — letting a roughly 40% hike probability go into a meeting without the pre-released press article that historically telegraphed moves — will structurally add volatility and uncertainty to markets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Higher rate-path uncertainty raises hedging costs and reinforces the lower-leverage regime, an argument for owning rate volatility.
insights.quote: I think this new no forward guidance going into the meeting, people had a 40% chance of a tightening, where in the past there'd have to be an article released beforehand to be a tightening.

insights.claim: Visser connects policy to system leverage: QE effectively levered the Fed's balance sheet by growing it whenever assets fell, so Warsh's intent to shrink it means the Fed itself delevers, compounding the decline in market leverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Removes the reflexive QE backstop under drawdowns, so dip-buying can no longer assume a policy put.
insights.quote: All of this leads to the same conclusion, which is there's going to be less leverage in the system.

insights.claim: Visser blames the K-shaped economy on post-GFC balance-sheet leverage in a financialized stock market and argues Fed delevering will improve wealth distribution, a view he believes Warsh and Bessent share as crypto and Bitcoin believers.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A policy regime aimed at Main Street over asset prices implies lower multiples but is structurally friendly to hard-asset and crypto allocations.
insights.quote: the K-shaped economy has been formed because of the leverage of the balance sheet

insights.claim: Visser says widening hyperscaler CDS reflects markets struggling to digest unprecedented short-term capital demand — SpaceX coming to market, upcoming lockup expiries, Anthropic and OpenAI raising for CapEx, Google's $80 billion deal — not credit deterioration on the world's best balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames hyperscaler spread widening as capital indigestion rather than default risk, making it something to fade rather than follow.
insights.quote: the leverage that is growing where CDS is going wider is on the best balance sheets in the world, the hyperscalers. That's why I'm not worried about them.

insights.claim: Visser argues tokenization will monetize dormant assets through fractionalization and daily liquidity, effectively releasing money supply and letting the Fed delever at the same time — a link he believes both Warsh and Bessent see — and expects rate cuts alongside opportunistic balance-sheet run-down once inflation and the labor market allow.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Connects crypto plumbing to monetary policy: tokenization becomes the mechanism that lets QT proceed without a liquidity crunch, with labor softness as the cut trigger.
insights.quote: tokenization will release money supply in a way that will allow the Fed to delever at the same time

themes.theme: Bitcoin and gold as the only durable store of value

insights.claim: Visser argues Bitcoin is arguably the best hedge fund ever created because its return profile mirrors Leopold's — including early 70-80% drawdowns — while continuing to compound, and that professional investors rejected it precisely because they 'knew' such returns were impossible.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes Bitcoin's volatility as the cost of a top-decile compounding stream, undercutting the drawdown-based objection allocators use.
insights.quote: arguably Bitcoin is the best hedge fund ever. Its returns look like Leopold's.

insights.claim: Visser predicts AI agents will allocate to Bitcoin where humans refused, because agents will probability-weight a new asset's returns and assign 5-20% rather than dismissing it on belief, driving crypto adoption sharply higher as agents take over transactions and investing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Identifies agentic portfolio construction as a specific, mechanical new bid for crypto from the currently 0%-allocated cohort.
insights.quote: those people that have 0% once agents start making decisions for them, the same thing that we've seen with the adoption here, the adoption of crypto will go through the roof

insights.claim: Visser is positioning in scarcity rather than growth — naming Micron, GE Vernova and Bitcoin — because this phase of innovation is energy-constrained, echoing David Friedberg's 'converting molecules into bits' framing and deliberately choosing the molecule side.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete allocation map: physical bottlenecks such as memory and power equipment plus hard money, rather than software beneficiaries.
insights.quote: So, scarcity's not just Bitcoin. Scarcity is Micron.

insights.claim: Visser reads Michael Saylor's 2021 pivot as driven by two forces — losing to competitive innovation against Microsoft-scale rivals with only a billion dollars on the balance sheet, and zero rates destroying returns on that cash — making Bitcoin a defense against debasement.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives the diagnostic for which corporates adopt Bitcoin treasuries next: squeezed competitive position plus idle cash earning nothing.
insights.quote: You don't find Bitcoin, Bitcoin finds you.

insights.claim: Visser predicts that within five years almost every business will be in MicroStrategy's 2021 position — squeezed by debasement and by hundreds of millions of AI-native competitors, since one person with an AI agent can launch 100 businesses — making store-of-value allocation a corporate necessity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames corporate treasury adoption of Bitcoin as a competitive-pressure inevitability, a structural demand source beyond ETF flows.
insights.quote: one person with an AI agent can set up 100 businesses

insights.claim: Asked what else qualifies as a store of value, Visser names only gold alongside Bitcoin, because AI's deflationary pressure eventually undermines the value of all businesses and assets once everything trends toward free.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Narrows the durable store-of-value universe to two assets, supporting a barbell of scarcity equities against gold and Bitcoin.
insights.quote: At some point, the deflationary pressures destroy all businesses and all assets because there's no need for the assets to be worth the value that they are if everything is heading towards free.

insights.claim: Visser positions Bitcoin at its current size relative to $700 trillion of global wealth as a hedge against his own AI-deflation scenario rather than a conviction bet, and says crypto should be about 5% of a diversified portfolio alongside real estate, private equity, private credit and public equities.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit sizing anchor — roughly 5% crypto as insurance — usable by allocators who reject the maximalist framing.
insights.quote: I think crypto needs to be 5%

themes.theme: Tokenized redistribution of the $700 trillion wealth pool

insights.claim: Visser's crypto valuation framework assumes total global wealth stays roughly fixed at about $703 trillion — $700 trillion non-crypto against $3 trillion crypto today — and that crypto reaches roughly $100 trillion within a decade purely through redistribution rather than aggregate growth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A large redistribution target with an explicit denominator, making the crypto bull case testable against outflows from other asset classes.
insights.quote: So crypto's going to end up being say $100 trillion in a decade. The rest of the assets of the world will still be 603 trillion

insights.claim: Visser expects public stock markets to be effectively unchanged in aggregate while private business valuations grow, because AI-native winners stay private with very few employees and founders retaining roughly 75% ownership, and a $100 million business no longer needs to scale to $5 billion.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If value accrues to closely held private companies, public-index beta is the wrong vehicle and private-access products become the growth business.
insights.quote: the public stock markets will be effectively unchanged, and private businesses will grow in their valuations

insights.claim: Visser predicts access to private value comes via tokenized ETFs covering every asset in the world, comparing the shift to ETFs themselves — which nobody believed in when he ran ETFs at Morgan Stanley in the early 2000s yet now dominate the market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tokenized wrappers on private assets are the structural growth product, and the ETF analogy sets expectations for how fast disbelief turns into dominance.
insights.quote: Tokenization is a massive change to the structure of the market. AI agents are a massive change, and all of this stuff is coming. It's a certainty.

insights.claim: Visser flags demographics as the transfer mechanism, noting the $700 trillion of global wealth is owned predominantly by baby boomers and people over 60 while the cohort inheriting it already embraces high-risk virtual and crypto participation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Generational wealth transfer is a slow, non-cyclical bid for crypto and virtual assets independent of any near-term catalyst.
insights.quote: the money of the world, the 700 trillion is owned predominantly by people that are baby boomers and people that are above the age of 60

themes.theme: Crypto rails: ETH breadth, stablecoins, borderless business

insights.claim: Visser reads Ethereum's outperformance of Bitcoin as a network-effect signal that crypto ecosystem energy is reviving despite Clarity Act fears, and notes his equal-weighted 40-name index spanning eight crypto verticals is also outperforming Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Breadth beyond ETH is the confirming signal; equal-weight alt outperformance versus BTC becomes a tradable regime indicator.
insights.quote: it's not just Ethereum, it's the eight verticals or sectors within inside crypto that are equal weight that are outperforming Bitcoin

insights.claim: Visser frames Ethereum as the crypto asset traditional finance money already knows, making it the safest choice relative to Solana or Sui for capital flowing out of the $700 trillion pool, while Bitcoin remains the store of value.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests an institutional two-asset barbell: BTC for store of value, ETH as the ecosystem bet with the least career risk.
insights.quote: think of Ethereum for me as the asset that most traditional finance people that have a lot of money already know. And so, it's the safest of the Solanas, the Suis

insights.claim: Visser's Ethereum bull case rests on consumer agents becoming real — matching up with Meta, Siri and Alexa — causing transaction volumes to explode where stablecoins and financial guardrails matter, with Stripe pursuing takeovers of transaction and volume businesses as corroborating evidence.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Names both the causal chain and the corporate tell (Stripe M&A) to monitor before positioning for on-chain volume growth.

insights.claim: Visser explicitly declines to underwrite Ethereum, Solana, Sui or BitTensor on a three-year horizon because AI will keep generating new ideas faster, so he only wants long-term exposure to assets not built on ideas — gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Separates a tactical ETH/altcoin trade from a durable holding, arguing altcoin exposure should be time-boxed rather than core.
insights.quote: 3 years from now, I don't know if Ethereum is safe on that. I don't know if Solana is safe on that. I don't know if Sui is. I don't know if BitTensor is.

insights.claim: Visser says dollar stablecoins have already solved the debasement motive for emigration — someone in Argentina facing 50% annual devaluation can simply hold dollar stablecoins, versus the black market he had to use in 1990s Brazil.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Structural, non-speculative stablecoin demand in high-inflation economies underpins volume growth independent of crypto price cycles.
insights.quote: if you want to stay in Argentina and the currency is devaluing 50% a year, you just put your money in stable coins, dollar stable coins, you're fine

insights.claim: Visser argues AI plus crypto removes the second historical reason for migration — access to an educated labor force — because a founder anywhere can now build a business with no employees, sell globally, collect revenue in stablecoins and let Stripe handle local tax.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Predicts geographic decoupling of business formation, expanding the addressable base for global payment rails and eroding labor-market arbitrage.
insights.quote: what has changed with AI connected to crypto is now you can build a business with no people

insights.claim: Visser cites Axie Infinity's measurable impact on the entire Philippine economy, alongside Fortnite's record growth, as proof that gaming-plus-economics virtual worlds already move real economies and that the pattern will recur as crypto and AI agents mature.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for consumer crypto reaching national-economy scale, supporting a revisit of gaming and digital-collectible infrastructure on the next adoption wave.
insights.quote: It impacted the entire economy of the Philippines.
